OPINION / MEDIA & ACCOUNTABILITY

Just how impartial is the BBC when it is staffed by uniparty civil servants?

39 civil servants over eight years. Government-paid staff helping produce BBC news. Taxpayers footing the wages—and licence-fee payers funding the broadcaster.

By Steve English · 19 October 2026 · The 39 figure is reported by The Telegraph [1]

The BBC insists it is independent. Yet government employees have been working inside its news operation while their departments continue paying their salaries.

And by “their departments”, we mean taxpayers.

The government’s own recruitment advert offered four three-month BBC placements for 2027. It specified that salaries would remain the responsibility of the employees’ departments, which could not recover that money from the BBC. [2]

Why should taxpayers subsidise staffing for a broadcaster that already receives licence-fee funding?

The arrangement spans Conservative and Labour governments. That is why I call it a uniparty arrangement: successive administrations accepted it. That is my criticism of the political establishment, not a claim that individual statisticians belong to either party.

The BBC says the scheme began in 2018. It has therefore continued across a change of government, while the public kept footing the bill. [5]

Government staff helping produce the news

These were contributions to political reporting and published news.

An ONS statistician described fact-checking Prime Minister’s Questions and party conferences, co-authoring a BBC article, and temporarily deputising for the BBC’s head of statistics. [3]

Another government statistician, working in BBC Verify, described assessing which government statistics deserved stories, advising on how information should be presented, and opportunities to “really influence stories”. Her account describes improving understanding and analysis, not instructions from ministers. [4]

The BBC says its journalists and editors retained editorial control. It also says the statisticians were required to present data objectively and resist political or commercial influence. But government employees were plainly contributing to the news audiences received. Who employed them and paid their wages should have been clear to those audiences. [5]

Those safeguards do not settle whether government-paid employees should be working inside the broadcaster’s news operation in the first place. Nor do they explain why the BBC should receive their services without reimbursing their departments.

Readers should not have to search government careers blogs to discover the employment arrangements behind people contributing to their news.

If someone helps analyse government figures for a BBC report, tell the audience clearly whether that person is employed by a government department. Let readers judge the arrangement for themselves.

You pay. The BBC receives the staff.

Taxpayers paid these employees’ salaries during their placements. Licence-fee payers funded the broadcaster benefiting from their work.

Two streams of public funding supported the same news operation.

And there is another unanswered question: who covered the work they left behind?

Did colleagues absorb it? Was it postponed? Were temporary workers or contractors hired? Was overtime paid?

Taxpayers were already paying these staff to work at the BBC, while licence-fee payers funded the content it produced. Were we also paying twice for their civil-service work—once for the absent employee and again for somebody to cover the job?

We do not yet know. Departments should publish the answer, along with any replacement staffing costs.

If replacement cover cost extra, publish the amount. If colleagues took on additional duties, explain the effect on their existing work. If projects were delayed, say which ones.

“Professional development” is an explanation for a placement. It is not, by itself, proof of value for money.

There may be useful skills to bring back. Show us what the departments expected to gain, how they assessed the benefit, and why taxpayers should meet the cost rather than the BBC.

These were authorised secondments. The employees had permission to go. Responsibility rests with the people who approved the arrangement and committed public resources to it.

Compulsory funding demands accountability

You can choose never to watch BBC television and still need a licence because you watch another broadcaster’s live programmes. BBC iPlayer also requires a licence. People who use neither generally do not need one, but the system still requires viewers of other live television services to help fund the BBC. [6]

A broadcaster funded on those terms should expect searching questions about its independence, spending and disclosure.

On 18 October, the BBC announced it was pausing the secondment programme and reviewing the arrangement. It said current secondees would not participate in publishing news or content during that review. [5]

That is a start.

Now publish every placement, its duration, its cost and the work undertaken. Explain what audiences were told. Disclose whether departments paid for replacement cover.

I do not need proof that a minister dictated a headline to question the judgment behind this scheme. The documented arrangement is enough to demand answers.

You paid the wages. You paid the licence fee. You deserve to know what you received—and who was doing the day job.

Sources & supporting evidence

Direct government accounts, recruitment terms, BBC reporting and the original investigation. No Spectator material used. Replacement-cover costs have not been established.

  1. The Telegraph investigation, 17 October 2026 — syndicated on AOL

    Source for the reported total of 39 civil servants over eight years and employment-disclosure concerns.

  2. Government Analysis Function — BBC secondment opportunities for 2027

    Recruitment terms: four three-month placements, departmental salaries and no BBC reimbursement. Page was indexed but returned an error when checked on 19 October 2026.

  3. Jodie Davis — Secondment to BBC News, 8 November 2021

    First-person account: PMQs, party conferences, co-authorship and deputising for the head of statistics.

  4. Masuma Ahmed — Ensuring Trust: My secondment to the BBC, 10 September 2024

    First-person account of work in BBC Verify, identifying stories and advising journalists.

  5. BBC News — BBC pauses civil service secondment scheme, 18 October 2026

    BBC report syndicated on AOL: programme pause, review, editorial-control statement and professional obligations.

  6. GOV.UK — TV Licence

    Live television and BBC iPlayer licensing requirements.
